newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions accept Kohl offer on coal subsidies.
newsitem.headline: German unions accept Kohl offer on coal subsidies.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl struck a deal with Germany's mining union on Thursday to avoid mass layoffs while slashing coal subsidies, convincing thousands of miners to end their protests and go home.

Bonn pledged to pump 900 million marks ($530 million) more than planned into the dying industry by the year 2000, but stuck to its plan to cut the annual level of federal subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) in 2005 from nine billion now.

Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told reporters: "We have ensured the survival of the mining industry in a way that is economically acceptable...We have ensured changes in the mining industry can be carried out in a way that avoids mass layoffs."

Miners' union boss Hans Berger hailed the deal as a success that would prevent feared forced layoffs among Germany's 90,000 miners, and ensure that 48,000 or so job losses would be cushioned with early retirement and retraining schemes.
"The fight was worth it," Berger said, adding that other union officials also believed the miners would accept the deal.
"This is the end of the struggle we started about a year ago," added union spokesman Christoph Meer. "The 13th of March is quite a good day in the history of the German mining union."

The miners had virtually besieged Bonn's government quarter for three days this week, but withdrew on Wednesday after Kohl postponed talks planned for Tuesday at short notice, saying he would not negotiate in a climate of intimidation.
Some 8,000 pit workers from Saar state on the French border who had taken part in the protests greeted the deal with cheers.
The men had spent the night in a tented village in the grounds of Cologne football stadium, ready to return the 30 km (20 miles) or so to Bonn if the deal was not to their liking.
Instead, most boarded a fleet of buses to go home, while several hundred miners on motorbikes roared through Bonn in a triumphal procession.

There were more mixed reactions in the main coal-and-steel district of the Ruhr valley, but the miners there appeared to be heeding the advice of their union to accept the deal, since there was no immediate move to restart the protests.

Germany's 18 pits stopped work last Friday after Bonn first announced the cuts, arguing that it could no longer afford to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is more than three times the world market price.
IG Bergbau had said the original plan would force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
The new plan may save two or three pits, while reducing annual German coal output to 30 million tonnes from 49 million.
In addition to the short-term help from the government, the mining employers and the state of North Rhine-Westphalia will also pump an extra 750 million marks into the industry by 2005.

The deal involves the Ruhr mining company Ruhrkohle taking over the Saar mines from Bonn and Saar state to rid Bonn of its loss-making majority stake and allow the restructuring to be conducted more efficiently.

The government said the new coal deal would have no effect on the 1997 budget, allaying worries that it might present a further obstacle in Germany's struggle to get its deficit within the limit allowed to qualify for European monetary union.
Last week the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who rule the two main mining states, walked out of talks with the government on potential cooperation on a major tax reform.
Peter Hintze, the general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats, said that after the deal "the SPD no longer has any excuse to refuse to cooperate on tax reform".

But SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine said Kohl's coalition would have to come up with new proposals to bring the SPD back to the bargaining table, above all to show it was ready to reduce the burden of wage deductions for social security. ($ = 1.695 German Marks)
